turns.content: Estimate the molar volume of CO2 at 500 K and 100 atm with the van der Waals model. Use a=3.610 atm dm^6 mol^-2 and b=0.0429 dm^3 mol^-1, in units compatible with R=0.082057 dm^3 atm mol^-1 K^-1.
Compute the ideal-gas comparison scale RT/p for this state, including its molar-volume units.
Starting from the molar van der Waals equation, use p for pressure, T for temperature, R for the gas constant, and a and T for the two van der Waals constants, then rearrange it into a cubic in V_m.
Substitute the stated constants, temperature, and pressure into the cubic. With x=V_m/(dm^3 mol^-1), write the numerical polynomial to be solved.
Check the units and signs of the cubic coefficients. Why must the van der Waals equation, rather than the ideal-gas value alone, be solved at this pressure?
Use the ideal-gas scale as a reference for identifying a gas-like solution. What qualitative criterion would distinguish the physical gas-phase root from any other numerical roots?
For the root selection, retain b=0.0429 dm^3 mol^-1 and explain the physical restriction V_m>b.
Use the numerical cubic to bracket a root in the physically admissible region and compare that interval with the ideal-gas scale.
Apply an appropriate numerical method to the cubic, list its real root candidates, and select the physical gas-phase root using V_m>b and the ideal-gas comparison.
Check the selected root by substitution into the cubic or the original van der Waals equation, and explain the direction of its deviation from RT/p.
Report the estimated van der Waals molar volume of CO2 with units and appropriate significant figures.
